A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same A2A-FM research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and can be matched despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic transport experiments, ZINC22 molecular optimization results, beta sensitivity analysis, and CelebA-Dialog HQ transfer examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports bin-count/runtime comparisons and a QED antisymmetry ablation result.

M1.justification: The coupling objective, flow-matching loss, training Algorithm 1, and ODE transport procedure are retained. The antisymmetric molecular vector-field formulation already appears in v1 Appendix B.2; its newly reported ablation does not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions use Gaussian-mixture and polar-coordinate synthetic data, ZINC22 QED and LogP–TPSA tasks, and CelebA-Dialog HQ beard/smile transfer. The grouped/non-grouped terminology and added bin-count analysis do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained in the corresponding synthetic and molecular comparisons. The synthetic comparator called Stochastic interpolants in v1 Table 1 is already identified as Multimarginal SI in its text. Additional SI bin counts are configurations of that existing comparator.

E3.justification: Algorithm 3 changes LogP–TPSA evaluation from similarity-threshold pooling to selecting the minimum-error attempt per target and averaging across targets. It also changes the stated noise intensity from 0.01 to 0.1, measures error against the target instead of the source, and excludes identity transfers. Appendix B.1 changes A2A-FM's synthetic batch size from 5,000 to 1,000. These are substantial reported protocol revisions, without establishing that the molecular experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an accuracy/runtime investigation of Multimarginal SI with K=2, 5, and 10, compared with A2A-FM and partial diffusion on common hardware (Appendix C, Figure 9, Table 6). Section 6 also newly reports a QED antisymmetry ablation. These expand the analysis to discretization, computational cost, and the architectural constraint; the existing beta sweep remains.

E5.justification: v1 Table 1 reports point estimates. v2 reports means and standard deviations over ten evaluations, with Appendix B.1 explaining the repeated evaluation procedure. This newly documents evaluation uncertainty, not ten independent training runs or an established increase in training seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the synthetic results: A2A-FM's continuous-condition MSE changes from 0.0101 to 0.0151 ± 0.0017, and its discrete coupling error from 0.0372 to 0.0581 ± 0.0222. These are revised estimates under changed reporting/settings, not established performance deterioration. Table 6 adds bin-count errors and training times; Section 6 adds 94.6% QED success without antisymmetry versus 97.5% with it. Tables 2–3 retain all molecular scores, including 97.5% success and 0.990 AUC.

T1.justification: Appendix A corrects the duplicated c2 penalty in v1 Equation 15 and replaces the inconsistent population-distribution construction with explicit projections of P ⊗ P in v2 Equation 17. It also makes finite-moment assumptions explicit. These repair the existing mathematical setup; the compactness-based convergence theorem and proof strategy remain.

C1.justification: v2's introduction adds an explicit claim that no prior method learns scalable all-to-all transfer from general observation–condition datasets. The central coupling, asymptotic optimal-transport, and molecular-performance contributions remain. Emphasizing grouped and non-grouped applicability largely clarifies scope already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses the beta/sample-size trade-off as a limitation, identifies theoretical justification of the heuristic as future work, and interprets antisymmetry as useful regularization. It removes v1's impact-statement qualification that metric-dependent transformations need not reflect reality and primarily support scientific exploration.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies V100 hardware, including one GPU for synthetic training and four for each molecular experiment. It also discloses 800 QED reference molecules and 100 condition-pair samples per synthetic evaluation, and adds configuration summaries and training times. The statement that code accompanies supplementary materials is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Meta Flow Matching, expands the distinction from conditional OT, and argues why simply substituting condition pairs into COT is insufficient. It adds references including Atanackovic et al., Peyré et al., and several molecular-property calculation works. The principal positioning against grouped-data transport methods remains.

P1.justification: The title changes, regressive-data terminology is replaced throughout by grouped/non-grouped framing, and substantial passages in the introduction, method explanation, related work, and experiments are rewritten. The molecular experiments are consolidated, an ablation subsection is introduced, and the appendix's ROC-style explanation is substantially shortened.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned, the synthetic figures are merged and rearranged, and v2 adds a QED task illustration, bin-count figure, and three tables. Existing molecular examples are reorganized, while the LogP–TPSA and face-transfer example collections are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The mathematical corrections, clearer exposition, synthetic uncertainty reporting, and new accuracy/runtime evidence make v2 easier to assess and better support its practical motivation. These gains are limited by unresolved molecular-evaluation reporting: Table 3 remains unchanged despite the rewritten Algorithm 3, whose minimum-selection rule can select zero-initialized entries from skipped trials. The revision therefore improves presentation and supporting evidence without clearly strengthening the principal molecular validation.
